note: You are reading the dialogue and narration written for the scenes of a visual novel — the lines characters speak and the on-screen narration, with scene/show staging. Judge only the writing on the page; you have no knowledge of the author's intent or any plan beyond what the lines show. Score on the scene's own register: a quiet, low-stakes exchange can reach the top level on its own terms, and a line is never better for being grand — figurative reach counts against a scene unless the speaker, setting, and moment earn it. Hear each line spoken aloud, not read on a page: HOW a person stages and orders their words — framing before the point, one idea at a time — matters as much as what they say, and a line that is grammatical but shaped for the page (compressed, front-loaded) is not how people talk. The top level is a scene a person would ship, not a flawless one. For each criterion, pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches the writing, and quote specific lines as evidence.

criteria.name: coherence
criteria._authoring: The why-chain / nonsense test — the single highest-value criterion and the easiest to wave through, because fluent nonsense passes every register and structure rule while meaning nothing. Anchored to the persistent generated attractor: lines that free-associate, name objects that do not belong in the scene's place, or answer an event that never happened. GATE: below level 2 this caps the overall at its own score — a scene of fluent nonsense cannot post a decent number on the strength of its craft.
criteria.description: Does every line survive the question 'why does that follow?' — react to the previous line's actual referent, name only things this scene has made real, and parse causally?

levels.0: Fluent nonsense. Lines are grammatical and in register but do not connect — they free-associate, reach for images or claims disconnected from what just happened, name objects that do not belong in this place, or answer events the scene never depicted. A reader cannot reconstruct why one line follows the last.
levels.1: Frequently unmoored. The through-line breaks often: several lines reference things the scene never established, or the causal link between exchanges is missing more than once or twice.
levels.2: Mostly tracks. The causal chain holds for most of the scene, with the occasional line that does not quite follow from the last or introduces a detail from nowhere.
levels.3: Coherent. Every line follows from the one before it; the objects and references all belong to this place and moment; a reader can always answer why a character said what they said.
levels.4: Watertight. The scene's causality is exact — each line is the natural consequence of what preceded it, grounded entirely in what the scene has made real, and nothing is arbitrary or free-associated.

criteria.name: voice_distinctness
criteria._authoring: Concrete test, not a vibe (it sat stuck at 3 for every run). The judge runs the cover-the-names test + counts swappable lines + checks for shared tics — checkable facts, not 'do they sound different'. NOTE this may legitimately stay flat when a cast is always-distinct by design (a loud one + a calm one); that is correct, not a miss — the discrimination shows across the genre battery (a same-register cast, a monovoice run).
criteria.description: Run the cover-the-names test: hide the speaker labels and try to place each line to its character by HOW it talks — rhythm, sentence length, word choice — not just what it is about. Then check (a) do two characters share a catchphrase, tic, or identical register, and (b) are there lines that could swap between characters with no loss? Count the unplaceable and swappable lines; quote examples. Characters who would genuinely share a voice (siblings, same upbringing) are exempt.

levels.0: One voice, many names. Names hidden, you cannot place lines at all — everyone shares sentence length, vocabulary, and temperature; most lines would swap freely between characters.
levels.1: Tagged, not voiced. Characters have a STATED difference (the nervous one, the gruff one) but it is not in the speech — names hidden, most lines are unplaceable and several could swap.
levels.2: Placeable by TOPIC only. You can often tell them apart by WHAT they discuss (their job, their worry) but not HOW they talk — rhythm and word-choice are shared, and some lines could still swap between them.
levels.3: Placeable by VOICE. Names hidden, you can usually place a line by its rhythm and word-choice, not just its subject; no two characters share a tic, and no line could swap to another mouth.
levels.4: Unmistakable. Any single line places its speaker on delivery alone, and moving any line to another character would break the scene.

criteria.name: naturalism
criteria._authoring: Concrete count, not a vibe. This is about word CHOICE only — a plain-but-flat or awkward line is NOT unnatural here (flatness belongs to flow, awkward staging to spoken_delivery), so naturalism can correctly stay high on plain writing and only bites when the prose gets writerly. That is why it is flat across a non-purple comedy cast and will bite on a purple horror/drama run — the genre battery is where it earns out.
criteria.description: Count the UNNATURAL lines — spoken lines a real person would not say aloud in conversation. Four tells: (a) figurative overshoot — a metaphor or simile no one uses in casual speech; (b) interiority spoken aloud — a character narrating their own inner state; (c) recited idea — a line stating a theme or concept out loud that no one would; (d) literary vocabulary — a word people write but don't speak. Count them and quote each. This is word CHOICE only: a plain or even flat line is NOT unnatural — do not count flatness or awkward staging here.

levels.0: Unnatural throughout. Stilted or uncanny as the default mode — sustained metaphor, interiority narrated aloud, recited ideas, or literary vocabulary across most exchanges.
levels.1: Three or more unnatural lines — repeated figurative overshoot, a recurring themed image, interiority spoken aloud, or hobby/job vocabulary used as emotional shorthand.
levels.2: One or two unnatural lines — mostly speakable, but a line or two reaches for an image or a written word where a person would just talk.
levels.3: Zero unnatural lines. Every line passes say-it-aloud; figurative language is rare and only on charged lines, never decorating ordinary ones.
levels.4: Zero unnatural lines, and the plainness is ALIVE — vivid exactly where feeling earns it, not merely inoffensive; the dialogue reads as effortlessly real.

criteria.name: spoken_delivery
criteria._authoring: The dimension the rubric was missing (added after the seed experiment). A line can be coherent, in-voice, and plain-worded yet still read WRITTEN, not SPOKEN — because its word ORDER and information-staging are shaped for the page. This is DISTINCT from naturalism (word CHOICE): judge the order and rhythm, not the vocabulary. Written tells: the payload front-loaded and compressed into tight apposition ('the bridge grunt in 2004, I was there'); a memory delivered as a compact fact instead of recalled loosely ('remember 2004? you died to the first grunt on the bridge'); several payloads crammed into one clipped line; the point stated with no framing a real speaker uses to stage it for a listener. Proven promptable — gold-seeded scenes unspool where unseeded AI lines compress.
criteria.description: Read each line as spoken aloud: is it SHAPED like talk — information staged in the order and rhythm a person actually uses (framing, topic-then-detail, one thing at a time) — rather than compressed into written word-order?

levels.0: Written throughout. Lines are grammatical but shaped for the page — payloads front-loaded and compressed, facts and callbacks stated in tight apposition, no speaker ever staging information the way talk does. Prose assigned to names.
levels.1: Frequently written. The shape tips into written-compression often — a memory delivered as a compact fact, two or three payloads crammed into one clipped line, the point stated before any framing — more than once or twice.
levels.2: Mixed. Some lines land as real speech, but several are ordered for the page — the information arrives compressed or front-loaded where a person would unspool it.
levels.3: Mostly spoken. Lines are staged the way people talk — framing before the point, one idea at a time, natural rhythm — with only the occasional line ordered like writing.
levels.4: Fully spoken. Every line is shaped as talk: information staged for a listener, the rhythm and word-order of real speech, never a line that reads as compressed prose.

criteria.name: flow
criteria._authoring: Scored by COUNTING concrete flow-breaks (not a vibe): the levels ladder on how many breaks the scene has, and each break type is a checkable thing the judge can point at. DISTINCT from coherence (line-to-line causality) and spoken_delivery (line word-order): flow is the SCENE holding together as one grounded moment. NOT 'importance' — a light slice-of-life scene has zero breaks just as easily as a dramatic one; never reward stakes or meaning here.
criteria.description: Does the scene hold together as one continuous, grounded moment? Look for concrete FLOW-BREAKS: (a) ungrounded opener — the first line drops into the middle of an exchange with no sense of who/where/what just happened; (b) flat affect-note — a narration line reporting a bare non-reaction as its own beat ('Marc doesn't blink'); (c) unconnected jump — the scene cuts from one activity to another with no line or action carrying you across; (d) orphan line — a line that neither answers the one before it nor is taken up by the one after. Count them, then pick the level. Quote each break you find.

levels.0: Fragments. Three or more flow-breaks, or the scene never finds its footing — ungrounded openers, unconnected jumps, and orphan lines throughout; it reads as assembled pieces, not a moment.
levels.1: Choppy. Two flow-breaks — e.g. an ungrounded opener plus a flat affect-note, or a jump between activities with no connective line and an orphan reply.
levels.2: One break. The scene mostly moves as a moment but has a single clear flow-break — one ungrounded jump, one orphan line, or one flat affect-note.
levels.3: Grounded. Zero flow-breaks: the scene opens with its footing, every line connects to its neighbors, and each shift of activity is carried by a line or action. It moves as one moment.
levels.4: Seamless. Zero breaks AND the motion is active — transitions do real work and the pacing varies naturally; the scene reads as lived, not merely unbroken.

criteria.name: subtext
criteria._authoring: Recalibrated after the seed experiment: the OLD L4 rewarded MAXIMAL indirection ('never states what it can show'), which pushes the model toward dense, loaded, oblique lines — the 'significance machine'. The real bar is EARNED subtext: mostly plain, direct talk, weight under the line only where the moment earns it. Over-obliqueness is now a failure, not the target. Level 0/1 still anchored to the 'diagnosis' attractor (a character explaining another's psychology back to them).
criteria.description: Do characters mostly talk plainly, with feeling carried UNDER the line — through what they avoid or deflect — at the moments that earn it, without either announcing emotions outright OR loading every line with hidden meaning?

levels.0: Everything announced. Characters state their emotions and goals outright as the default, or diagnose each other — explaining the other person's fears and motives back to them; nothing left to infer.
levels.1: Mostly on the nose. Feelings are usually named directly, or one character narrates what another 'really' feels.
levels.2: Uneven. Some beats carry subtext, but the scene either declares feelings flatly in places OR strains for loaded meaning where plain talk would do.
levels.3: Well-judged. Mostly plain, direct talk, with feeling carried under the line at the charged moments; the scene trusts the player to read the beats that matter.
levels.4: Exactly weighted. Plain where people are plain, and the weight lands under the line precisely when the moment earns it — never announcing emotion, and never the 'significance machine' where every line strains to mean something.

criteria.name: scene_economy
criteria._authoring: Recalibrated after the seed experiment: the OLD levels treated any restatement/looseness as filler, which fights spoken_delivery — real speech stages and restates to land a point, and that is WORK, not waste. Waste is a line that does NOTHING (dramatic OR spoken). Never grade line count; length is not a defect signal.
criteria.description: Does every line do real work — advancing tension, revealing character, moving the situation, OR making the talk sound spoken — with no dead lines? Natural framing, staging, and the way people restate to land a point are WORK; waste is a line that does nothing at all.

levels.0: Dead lines throughout. Lines exist only to fill space — empty back-and-forth carrying no information, feeling, or spoken texture; whole exchanges could vanish with no loss.
levels.1: Much dead weight. Some lines work, but the scene is laced with exchanges that carry nothing — not information, not character, not the rhythm of real talk.
levels.2: Genuinely inert in places. The scene gets where it is going, but several lines do nothing — restating known facts to no effect (as opposed to the natural restating that stages a point).
levels.3: Tight but human. Nearly every line earns its place — through drama OR spoken texture — and cutting one would cost information, tension, character, or naturalness.
levels.4: Nothing dead. Every line does at least one job — dramatic or making the scene sound spoken — and none is inert; lean without being clipped into written compression.

criteria.name: beat_fidelity
criteria._authoring: Close discipline folded in — the known attractor is a scene that ends by stating its own theme aloud; a good close is an action or a short in-voice line.
criteria.description: Does each node read as a complete, coherent scene — a clear event with consistent characters and place — and end well: correctly for its node type (a menu for a branch, a jump for a linear node) and without stating its own theme aloud?

levels.0: Broken. The node has no coherent scene — fragments, a place or cast that shifts mid-scene, or a missing/contradictory ending (a branch with no menu, a node that dead-ends).
levels.1: Barely holds. A scene is discernible but underbaked — it gestures at an event without depicting it, the ending type is wrong, or it closes by announcing what it all meant.
levels.2: Functional. A clear scene with the right ending, but generic — it advances the situation without a specific event, revelation, or decision landing.
levels.3: Delivers. The node depicts a specific event, exchange, or decision with a consistent cast and place, ends correctly for its type, and closes on an action or a line rather than a thematic summary.
levels.4: Lands cleanly. The node delivers a sharp, specific scene whose ending — menu or jump — feels like the natural result of the lines that built to it, and whose last line trusts the player.
